# Nehemiah Chapter 5 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 471v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/NEH_005_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Around this time, a fierce protest erupted among the common people and their wives — directed against their own Jewish countrymen.

**2** Some cried out, "We have large families to feed! We need grain just to survive!"

**3** Others said, "We've had to mortgage our fields, our vineyards, and even our homes just to buy food during this famine."

**4** Still others said, "We've had to borrow money to pay the king's taxes on our fields and vineyards.

**5** We are flesh and blood just like our wealthy neighbors — our children are no different from theirs. Yet we are being forced to sell our sons and daughters into slavery! Some of our daughters have already been taken, and there is nothing we can do. Our fields and vineyards now belong to others."

**6** When I heard their outcry and these stories, I burned with anger.

**7** After thinking it through carefully, I confronted the nobles and officials head-on: "You are exploiting your own people by charging them interest!" Then I called a large public assembly to address the matter.

**8** I said to them, "We have done everything we could to buy back fellow Jews who were sold into slavery among foreign nations. And now you are selling your own people — only for them to be bought back by us again!" They had nothing to say; they stood in silence.

**9** I continued, "What you are doing is wrong. Don't you fear God? You are giving our enemies — the surrounding nations — reason to mock us!

**10** I myself, along with my brothers and servants, have been lending money and grain. But let us stop charging interest.

**11** Give back their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses today. And return the interest you have charged — the percentage on the money, grain, wine, and olive oil."

**12** They answered, "We will give it all back. We will demand nothing more from them. We will do exactly as you say." So I summoned the priests and made the nobles and officials take a solemn oath to keep their word.

**13** Then I shook out the folds of my robe and declared, "May God shake out every person who breaks this promise — shake them out of their homes and away from everything they have worked for. May they be left with nothing!" The whole assembly shouted "Amen!" and praised the LORD. And the people kept their promise.

**14** Furthermore, during the entire twelve years I served as governor of Judah — from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes — neither I nor my family ever drew on the governor's food allowance.

**15** The governors before me had been a heavy burden on the people, taking food, wine, and forty shekels of silver from them. Even their assistants exploited the people. But I refused to do this, out of reverence for God.

**16** I also devoted myself personally to the wall construction. We did not acquire any land for ourselves, and all my servants joined in the building work.

**17** Every day, a hundred and fifty Jewish officials ate at my table, plus visitors from the surrounding nations.

**18** The daily provisions I provided were: one ox, six premium sheep, poultry, and every ten days a generous supply of wine. Despite this enormous expense, I never demanded the governor's food allowance, because the people were already burdened enough.

**19** Remember me favorably, O my God, for everything I have done for this people.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes
1. **Internal injustice during external threat** — The timing is devastating: even as enemies threaten from outside, the wealthy within are exploiting their own people. Nehemiah recognizes that a community divided by economic injustice cannot withstand external attack.
2. **Covenant economics** — Nehemiah's reform is not merely political; it is rooted in Torah. The prohibition on interest between Israelites (Exod 22:25; Lev 25:36) was designed to prevent the cycle of debt-slavery that erased the Exodus liberation. Nehemiah is restoring the Exodus ethic.
3. **The "remember me" prayer** — Nehemiah's closing plea (v. 19) is not self-righteousness but covenant logic: he has acted faithfully and asks God, the covenant partner, to take notice. This prayer recurs throughout the book as Nehemiah's personal signature.

*— PNEUMA*
